systemsMapSummary: Under-reporting is held in place by three reinforcing loops: a friction loop (the only channel is a 15-minute paper form kept by the office, not the machine), a black-hole loop (supervisors rarely follow up, so operators who reported 'never heard back' and stop bothering), and a fear loop (the shift bonus's 'zero-incident' component makes a report feel like it dents the team's payout). Hard to report, plus nothing changes when you do, plus a reason not to, equals about four reports a month against a floor of 180 operators.
headline: If reporting took two minutes at the machine, every report visibly led to action, and it couldn't dent the bonus, we'd likely see near-miss reports rise from ~4 toward a healthy leading-indicator rate — a sign risk is surfacing earlier, not that the plant got less safe.

loops: Friction loop: hard-to-use form -> fewer reports -> reporting stays invisible -> the form stays a low priority to fix -> still hard to use.
Black-hole loop: no follow-up -> reporting feels pointless -> fewer reports -> supervisors see little to action -> follow-up never becomes routine.

strongestBarriers.barrier: The only channel is a slow form kept away from the line
strongestBarriers.rationale: Highest impact and highly changeable; a tear-off card at the machine removes the walk and the wait that suppress most reports.

strongestBarriers.barrier: Reports vanish, so operators believe reporting is pointless
strongestBarriers.rationale: High impact; visibly closing the loop is what converts a one-off report into a habit.

strongestBarriers.barrier: The bonus and mild social risk make reporting feel costly
strongestBarriers.rationale: Reframing reporting as valued, and decoupling it from the bonus, removes the strongest reason to stay quiet.

barrierNarratives.point: Put a fast, tear-off report card at every machine
barrierNarratives.narrative: The report has to survive the moment it's needed. A two-minute card at the machine removes the walk to the office and the 15-minute form — it takes friction away rather than adding a rule, and an operator already asked for exactly this.

barrierNarratives.point: Close the loop visibly — acknowledge every report and show what changed
barrierNarratives.narrative: A report that 'goes into a black hole' teaches operators not to bother. Acknowledging every report and showing what changed is what turns a single report into a habit, because effort finally has a visible payoff.

barrierNarratives.point: Separate near-miss reporting from the shift bonus so it can't cost the team
barrierNarratives.narrative: As long as a near-miss can dent the team's payout, the rational move is silence. Decoupling reporting from the bonus removes the strongest reason not to report, so the other levers can work.

gapLog.content: The low report rate reflects suppressed reporting rather than genuinely few near-misses — the rising injury trend supports this but does not prove it.
Time from report to action is not tracked, so the 'black hole' barrier is described by operators but not yet measured.
Confirm exactly how the shift bonus treats near-misses (policy doc not attached) — whether a report affects the bonus, or only a recordable injury does.
The 10-20 near-misses per recordable benchmark was heard at a forum, not a cited source — treat as directional.

discoveryActivities: 6-8 short interviews with operators across all three shifts to confirm whether friction, futility, or fear suppresses reporting most.
A walkthrough timing the current paper-form process from the line to the office to quantify the reporting friction.
Review a sample of past reports to see how many received any documented follow-up, establishing the report-to-action baseline.
Clarify with Operations how the 'zero-incident' bonus component actually treats near-misses, and whether operators' belief matches the policy.
